tier_reason: First-party page lists the CPU (Core i5-4690K, SSD), flags (-g -O2 -MD / -MD), ccache 3.7.1 and median-of-100 method, and the repo has a timing script (misc/performance). But the page never names the compiler or its version, and it does not link the script, so this is not tier A. First-party numbers with partial methodology are tier C.

corrections.baseline: Uncached compilation (same compiler command run without ccache); the page does not involve Make/Ninja and does not name the compiler
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Compiler not named on page; -g -O2 -MD plus needed -I flags (ccache.c); -MD only (c++_includes.cc); ccache 3.7.1
corrections.hardware: Intel Core i5-4690K, standard SSD, Linux desktop
corrections.caveats: Measures single-file cache hits against a plain uncached compile, not an end-to-end Make/Ninja build, so real speedup depends on hit rate. Cache misses are slower than no cache: first-time runs were 0.96-0.98x (ccache.c) and 0.83-0.97x (c++_includes.cc), and the page cites 5-20% miss overhead (1-3% in depend mode). The page does not name the compiler or give a date. It was measured with the old ccache 3.7.1 on a dated i5-4690K. ccache is itself a named baseline of the compile-caching-and-distribution category.

notes: All six speedup factors match the page exactly. The downgrade is only because the compiler is unnamed; the rest of the methodology is solid. The GPL-3.0-or-later license is confirmed from LICENSE.adoc (gh shows NOASSERTION), and stars are 2,961.

tier_reason: The benchmark configs are public (example/thirdparty/netty/build.mill and example/thirdparty/mockito/build.mill), and the page lists the exact timed commands and flags, e.g. './mvnw -T 10 -Pfast -Denforcer.skip=true install' vs './mill __.compile'. It also states Java 17 + Mill 0.12.9-native and the machine (2021 M1 MacBook Pro, 10 CPU, 32GB), so the build configuration and machine are fully specified.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Java 17 (javac), Mill 0.12.9-native; Maven/Gradle at each project's default version; exact timed commands and flags listed on page (e.g. ./mvnw -T 10 -Pfast -Denforcer.skip=true install; ./mill -j1 __.compile)
corrections.hardware: 2021 M1 MacBook Pro, 10 CPU cores, 32GB RAM (exact M1 variant not named)
corrections.caveats: Baseline is Maven/Gradle, not one of this run's named baselines (CMake+Ninja, Make, Bazel, Cargo). These are Mill's own ad-hoc numbers (median wall time of 3 runs after warmup). The page contradicts itself on versions: a general note says Mill 1.1.0, but the in-depth sections that hold the tables say Java 17 + Mill 0.12.9-native. Maven/Gradle versions are the project defaults and are not pinned. The Mill ports of Netty and Mockito are incomplete: some subprojects and linters are disabled for the comparison.

notes: All ten speedup figures (Netty/Maven and Mockito/Gradle) match the page. The license (MIT), 2.8k stars (2,795) and last commit (2026-09-24) are confirmed.

tier_reason: The README gives one first-party number: 'up to 2x faster than Buck1 in practice', from internal Meta usage. It gives no workload, hardware, method or benchmark code. That is a number without methodology, so tier C.

corrections.caveats: The README footnote says the figure 'comes from internal usage of Buck1 versus Buck2 at Meta' and that 'appropriate comparisons with systems like Bazel have yet to be performed; Buck1 is the baseline because it's simply what existed and what had to be replaced.' Buck1 is not one of this run's named baselines (CMake+Ninja, Make, Bazel, Cargo), and the 2x figure has no stated workload, hardware or methodology.

notes: The claim matches the README. The license is dual MIT and Apache-2.0 (LICENSE-MIT and LICENSE-APACHE), even though gh shows only Apache-2.0. Stars (4,438) and last commit (2026-09-24) are confirmed. The only correction completes the truncated verbatim quote in caveats.

tier_reason: A first-party page describes the synthetic generator setup ('make -rR', N = 1 to 100k) and shows log-log graphs. It states no CPU, OS or compiler flags, and the generator script is not published. The gain is also implausible-looking (about 30 min vs 0.1 s), so tier C.

corrections.caveats: First-party page with no CPU model, OS or compiler flags stated, and the generator script is not published. The ratio (about 30 min vs 0.1 s) looks implausible, so it is capped at tier C under the >50x rule. The page footer shows a 2008-2024 copyright, so the hardware is likely old. At 100k files the log-scale graphs appear to put make at a little over 1,000 s (about 20 min), which is below the text's 'half an hour'. The near-zero no-op and update times rely on tup's file monitor, which took 9.7 s to start the first time at 200k files and 2 min 30 s with a cold cache (2.5 s hot). The 100k-file case is a stress test, and tup's cold build is 5-30% slower than make.

notes: The text states make takes 'a half an hour' vs tup 'a tenth of a second' for a single C-file change at 100k files, tup takes '0 seconds' for nothing-changed, and tup is 5-30% slower on the initial build. The make no-op value comes from the graph and the general '30 minutes per update for make' remark. GPL-2.0 (COPYING), 1,262 stars and last commit 2026-07-30 are confirmed.

tier_reason: The README's Benchmark section gives first-party timings for building the in-repo xmake-core (core/) with xmake, ninja, cmake+make and cmake+ninja. It gives only '8core' for hardware, with no CPU model, compiler or flags, and no benchmark script. That is tier C.
notes: Every raw time matches the README, and the derived ratios check out (1.36x, 1.24x, 1.155x, 1.075x). The cmake+make totals include the generate step; make alone vs xmake is about 1.14x on both -j12 runs (derived from page data). License (Apache-2.0), 12,231 stars and last commit 2026-09-22 on the default branch 'dev' are confirmed.
